stem_html:
The evidence for the earliest domestication of the horse remains ______. Bit wear on a tooth can be produced by a rope halter as easily as by a bridle, and the size change usually cited appears in wild herds under the same climate pressure.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "equivocal"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "abundant", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "fabricated", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "recent", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Quantity against quality. The sentence is about what the evidence proves, not how much of it there is.
  • Ambiguity is not fraud.
  • Two examples, one shape. Each has an alternative cause, which is the pattern the blank must name.

Why A is right Each piece of evidence is shown to have a second explanation: bit wear on a tooth can be produced by a rope halter as easily as by a bridle. Evidence that points two ways at once is equivocal.

Why B is wrong Abundant counts the evidence, and the sentence is about what the evidence shows. Two independent lines are described, and both are inconclusive rather than scarce.

Why C is wrong Fabricated accuses somebody of inventing the data. The passage says the observations are real and admit an innocent explanation.

Why D is wrong Recent dates the evidence rather than evaluating it, and no chronology of the research appears.

stem_html:
Rather than ______ the disagreement between the two datasets, Osei's paper builds on it: the chapter that reconciles them is the shortest in the book, and the three chapters that follow use the gap to locate an instrument fault nobody had suspected.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "minimizing"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "exploiting", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "documenting", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "compounding", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Rather than” inverts. One choice restates what follows the colon.
  • The short chapter is the evidence, and its shortness is the point.
  • A neutral verb where the sentence needs a dismissive one.

Why A is right “Rather than” requires the opposite of what the paper does, and what it does is build on the disagreement. Treating it as small is the alternative it rejects, and the short reconciling chapter is the sign of the path not taken.

Why B is wrong Exploiting is a synonym for building on it, so the sentence would say the paper did the thing it is contrasted with.

Why C is wrong Documenting is neutral and is something the paper plainly does; the chapter that reconciles the datasets records the disagreement.

Why D is wrong Compounding would mean making the disagreement worse, which is neither what the paper does nor an alternative it declines.

stem_html:
The building's facade is ______: the columns carry nothing, the pediment sits in front of a steel frame that holds the roof up on its own, and the stone is a skin four centimetres thick.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "ornamental"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "unstable", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "derivative", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "unfinished", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Non-structural is not unsound. The frame is doing the work.
  • The classical vocabulary invites a comment on style, and the evidence is entirely about load-bearing.
  • Three details, one property.

Why A is right Three details say the same thing: the columns carry nothing, the frame holds the roof up on its own, and the stone is four centimetres thick. A facade that does no structural work is there to be looked at.

Why B is wrong Unstable would mean the building is at risk, and the sentence says the opposite — the steel frame holds the roof up perfectly well.

Why C is wrong Derivative would say the design copies something. Columns and a pediment do suggest a borrowed vocabulary, but the evidence given is about load, not about sources.

Why D is wrong Unfinished contradicts a facade with stone cladding and a pediment in place. Nothing suggests work remains.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2020 article about food labelling.

Front-of-pack warning labels are evaluated by whether shoppers can recall them, and on that measure the octagonal black label used in Chile performs superbly. Tabares tracked purchases rather than recall and found that the label changed what manufacturers made more than it changed what shoppers bought: within two years, reformulation had removed the label from a third of products, while the share of labelled products in the average basket barely moved. The label worked, she argues, but not through the shopper.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It names a standard measure of success, reports a study using a different measure, and states what that study implies about how the policy works."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It compares two labelling schemes and argues that one is more memorable than the other.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It describes a policy and lists the objections manufacturers have raised to it.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It reports a study and explains why its method is unreliable.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which method the passage endorses. One choice reverses it.
  • Manufacturers reformulating is the finding, not a complaint.
  • The last sentence is a conclusion about mechanism, which is the third move.

Why A is right Three moves in order: recall as the usual measure, Tabares tracking purchases instead, and the conclusion that the label worked but not through the shopper.

Why B is wrong One label is discussed, not two, and memorability is the criterion the passage sets aside rather than the one it applies.

Why C is wrong No manufacturer objects anywhere in the text. Manufacturers appear as the party that reformulated.

Why D is wrong The passage treats Tabares's method as the better one. It criticises the standard measure, not her study.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from Frederick Douglass's 1855 autobiography My Bondage and My Freedom.

I have found that, to make a contented slave, it is necessary to make a thoughtless one. It is necessary to darken his moral and mental vision, and, as far as possible, to annihilate the power of reason. He must be able to detect no inconsistencies in slavery; he must be made to feel that slavery is right; and he can be brought to that only when he ceases to be a man.

Which choice best describes the function of the final clause in the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It states the cost of the process the passage has described, framing that process as the destruction of a person."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It identifies the specific methods enslavers used to prevent education.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It concedes that some enslaved people did come to accept their condition.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It shifts the passage from argument to personal recollection.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A conditional read as an admission. “Only when” sets a price, it does not report a sale.
  • Requirements against methods.
  • The first-person frame is in the first sentence, so nothing shifts at the end.

Why A is right The passage builds a sequence of requirements — thoughtless, darkened vision, no detected inconsistencies — and the final clause names what they add up to: he can be brought to that only when he ceases to be a man.

Why B is wrong No method is named. The passage describes what has to be achieved, not how it was done.

Why C is wrong The clause states a condition, not a concession: contentment is possible only at a price that has not been paid. It denies rather than admits.

Why D is wrong The passage opens with “I have found,” so the personal frame is there from the first sentence and the final clause continues the argument.

stem_html:
Text 1

Musicians who train from childhood outperform non-musicians on tests of auditory attention. The training explanation is straightforward: years of distinguishing a second violin from a viola sharpen the auditory system, and the advantage transfers to speech in noise.

Text 2

Kaur followed 900 children from age five. Those who went on to study music for a decade already scored above average on auditory attention at age five, before any lessons began, and their scores improved at the same rate as everyone else's over the decade that followed.

Based on the texts, how would Kaur (Text 2) most likely characterize the explanation offered in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "As mistaking a pre-existing difference for an effect of the training."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "As correct about the cause but wrong about the size of the advantage.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "As failing to account for children who abandon music lessons early.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "As underestimating how much auditory attention improves with training.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Selection against effect. The advantage is real and it predates the cause proposed for it.
  • Two findings, both needed. The baseline difference alone would not settle it; the equal improvement rates do.
  • A quibble about size where the disagreement is about direction of causation.

Why A is right Kaur's two findings remove the causal claim: the future musicians already scored above average at age five, before any lessons began, and their scores improved at the same rate as everyone else's. The gap existed first and the training did not widen it.

Why B is wrong She does not accept the cause. Her data leave the training with no measured effect at all, which is a disagreement about cause rather than about magnitude.

Why C is wrong Dropouts are never mentioned in Text 2. Her sample is defined by who went on to study for a decade.

Why D is wrong This reverses her finding, which is that improvement was no faster among the musicians.

stem_html:
Agronomist Chiara Bellini hypothesized that intercropping maize with beans raises maize yield because the beans fix nitrogen the maize can use, rather than because the beans suppress weeds.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Bellini's hypothesis?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Maize intercropped with beans out-yielded weeded maize monoculture given the same fertiliser, but not maize monoculture given extra nitrogen."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Maize intercropped with beans out-yielded unweeded maize monoculture.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Plots intercropped with beans carried fewer weeds than maize monoculture plots did.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Beans grown alone fixed measurable quantities of nitrogen in the soil.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The rival has to be controlled, not confirmed. One choice measures the rival and calls it support.
  • A control that leaves the confound in place.
  • Half a mechanism. Fixation without uptake proves nothing about yield.

Why A is right Weeding the monoculture removes the weed explanation, and adding nitrogen to a second monoculture removes the yield advantage. Together they show the beans are acting as a nitrogen source, which is what the hypothesis says: the beans fix nitrogen the maize can use.

Why B is wrong An unweeded control leaves weed suppression free to explain the whole result, which is the alternative Bellini is arguing against.

Why C is wrong Fewer weeds supports the explanation she rejects. It is evidence for the rival, presented as though it were evidence for her.

Why D is wrong That beans fix nitrogen is half of the mechanism and is not in dispute. The question is whether the maize gets the benefit.

stem_html:
A historian argues that the printed sermons of a seventeenth-century preacher were composed for readers rather than transcribed from the pulpit, on the grounds that a text written for the page will use constructions the ear cannot follow.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the historian's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The printed sermons contain long parenthetical clauses and cross-references to earlier pages, neither of which appears in surviving stenographic records of the same preacher's delivered sermons."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The printed sermons were issued by a publisher who also printed the works of several other preachers.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The printed sermons are longer than the average sermon delivered in the period.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Stenographic records of the preacher's delivered sermons survive for only two occasions.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The argument names its own test. Evidence that does not address it cannot support it.
  • Quantity where the criterion is kind.
  • A limitation offered as a finding.

Why A is right The historian's test is stylistic: a text written for the page will use constructions the ear cannot follow. Parentheses and page cross-references are exactly such constructions, and their absence from the spoken records completes the comparison.

Why B is wrong Who printed them says nothing about how they were composed. A publisher's list is not evidence about style.

Why C is wrong Length is suggestive and does not meet the stated test, since a long sermon can still be entirely followable by ear.

Why D is wrong The scarcity of stenographic records is a limitation on the evidence, not support for the argument.

stem_html:
A team measured germination rates for seeds of one plant species collected at four elevations and grown together in a single greenhouse. They concluded that the differences in germination are inherited rather than caused by the growing conditions.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the team's conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Germination fell steadily from 82 percent to 48 percent as source elevation rose, even though every seed was grown in the same greenhouse."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Seeds from 400 m germinated at 82 percent, the highest rate recorded.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Germination rates for all four source elevations were above 45 percent.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Seeds from 1900 m germinated at a lower rate than seeds from 1400 m.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The common greenhouse is half the argument, and only one choice mentions it.
  • One bar or one pair is not a trend.
  • A true reading with no bearing on the claim.

Why A is right The conclusion needs a difference that tracks origin while the environment is held constant, and that is what the graph shows: a steady fall across four source elevations for seeds grown together in a single greenhouse.

Why B is wrong One bar's height is not a pattern, and by itself it says nothing about inheritance.

Why C is wrong A floor that all four clear is unrelated to either half of the conclusion.

Why D is wrong A single pairwise comparison is consistent with the pattern and does not establish it, and it omits the shared growing conditions that make the conclusion possible.

stem_html: In her novel Winterline, Oyelaran presents the grandmother as a character who converts every question about the past into a practical instruction about the present. Which quotation from a fictional novel would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“I asked her what the village had been called before. She said the kettle was boiling and I should take it off before it spat.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“I asked her what the village had been called before, and she told me, and then she told me the name of every family in it.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“She never spoke of the village, and I learned not to ask, and the silence sat between us like a third person.”", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“She said the past was a country she had left, and that people who go back to such countries do not come home again.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Refusal against redirection. The claim names a specific move, not reticence.
  • A statement about the past is still an answer about the past.
  • The instruction has to be practical and immediate, which is what makes the kettle the right detail.

Why A is right The question is about the past and the answer is a task for right now, which is the conversion the claim describes: a question about the past turned into a practical instruction about the present.

Why B is wrong Here she answers the question about the past at length. That is the opposite of converting it.

Why C is wrong Silence is a refusal rather than a conversion. Nothing is turned into an instruction; the question is simply never asked.

Why D is wrong This is a statement of principle about the past, and it is neither practical nor an instruction. It explains an attitude instead of enacting one.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2023 article about wildfire policy.

A century of suppression has left western forests with several times the stem density they carried in 1900, and prescribed burning is the standard remedy. Ruvalcaba's survey of burn programmes in six states finds that the acreage treated each year is set almost entirely by the number of days when wind, humidity and staffing all permit ignition — a number that has fallen as fire seasons have lengthened. Funding, she notes, was never the binding constraint: in four of the six states the programmes returned money.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "What limits prescribed burning is the shrinking number of days on which it can safely be done, not the money available for it."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Western forests carry several times the stem density they carried in 1900.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Prescribed burning programmes in six states have been underfunded for decades.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Fire seasons in the western United States have lengthened.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • One choice states the reverse of an explicit sentence.
  • Background against claim. The first sentence explains the need for the policy.
  • A cause promoted to the thesis.

Why A is right The passage identifies the real constraint — the number of days when wind, humidity and staffing all permit ignition — and rules out the assumed one: funding was never the binding constraint.

Why B is wrong The stem density is the setup that explains why burning is wanted at all.

Why C is wrong The passage says the opposite: in four of the six states the programmes returned money.

Why D is wrong The lengthening fire season is a cause of the shrinking window, mentioned inside a dash. It is a step in the argument, not the argument.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about the mathematician Sophie Germain.

Germain corresponded with Gauss under a man's name for three years, and the story is usually told as one of concealment. Her letters to Legendre, published in full in 2019, show a different practice: to Legendre she wrote as herself from the beginning, and the two argued about elasticity for a decade. Germain chose her disguise correspondent by correspondent, and she chose it where she judged the mathematics would not otherwise be read.

According to the text, what do Germain's letters to Legendre indicate?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Her use of a pseudonym was selective rather than a uniform practice."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "She concealed her identity from every mathematician she corresponded with.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Legendre was more receptive to her work than Gauss was.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Her work on elasticity was more significant than her work in number theory.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A counterexample read as the rule.
  • The passage judges her practice, not her correspondents.
  • Two fields named, and neither is ranked.

Why A is right The Legendre letters are the counterexample: to Legendre she wrote as herself from the beginning. The passage generalises that she chose her disguise correspondent by correspondent.

Why B is wrong This is the usual telling that the letters overturn. The Legendre correspondence is precisely a case where she did not conceal.

Why C is wrong Gauss's receptiveness is never described, and her judgement about who would read the mathematics is her own, not a report about him.

Why D is wrong No comparison of significance between her two areas of work appears.

stem_html:
A species of orchid is pollinated by a single moth species whose tongue is as long as the orchid's nectar spur. On one island the moth is absent, yet the orchid sets seed at the same rate as on islands where the moth is present, and the seeds are genetically identical to the parent plant. Since no other insect on the island can reach the nectar, it can be concluded that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the island population reproduces without cross-pollination."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "a second moth species on the island has evolved a comparably long tongue.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the orchid's nectar spur is shorter on the island than elsewhere.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the orchid will not survive on the island in the long term.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two facts, and the answer has to use both. Identical seed is the one that rules out every pollinator.
  • Contradicting a premise. Two choices need an insect the passage has excluded.
  • A prediction rather than an inference.

Why A is right Seeds genetically identical to the parent cannot have two parents, and seed set continues where no pollinator can reach the nectar. Reproduction without cross-pollination is the only reading the two facts allow.

Why B is wrong The passage rules this out: no other insect on the island can reach the nectar. It would also produce genetically varied seed rather than identical seed.

Why C is wrong A shorter spur would make the nectar reachable, which contradicts the premise, and it would still not explain seeds identical to the parent.

Why D is wrong Long-term survival is not addressed. The population is currently setting seed at the same rate as elsewhere.

stem_html:
Two hospitals report their surgical mortality rates. Hospital A's overall rate is higher than Hospital B's. Within every category of case severity, however, Hospital A's rate is lower than Hospital B's, and Hospital A treats a far larger share of the most severe cases. It follows that Hospital A's higher overall rate ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "reflects the mix of cases it treats rather than worse outcomes for comparable patients."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "shows that its surgeons perform worse than Hospital B's on severe cases.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "means that Hospital B should take more severe cases.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "indicates that the two hospitals define severity differently.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The overall figure and every subgroup point opposite ways. The mix is what reconciles them.
  • Reading the overall rate as the outcome measure when the categories already control for severity.
  • A conclusion about policy from a conclusion about numbers.

Why A is right Hospital A does better in every severity category and takes more of the hardest cases. The only way it can still be worse overall is that the harder mix pulls its total up.

Why B is wrong Within every category A's rate is lower, including the severe ones, so this contradicts a stated fact.

Why C is wrong A recommendation about which hospital should take which cases does not follow from the mortality figures alone.

Why D is wrong Different definitions would undermine the comparison, and the passage gives no hint of it. The categories are treated as shared.

stem_html:
The kiln reached its working temperature in eleven hours ______ who fire with wood usually allow twice that.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; potters"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", potters", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "potters", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": potters", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Both halves stand alone.
  • A colon for a fact that merely relates.
  • The second clause opens with a noun, which makes it read as a continuation of the first.

Why A is right Two independent clauses stand on either side of the blank with no conjunction between them, and a semicolon is the mark that joins them.

Why B is wrong A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice.

Why C is wrong No punctuation fuses the sentences and briefly attaches “potters” to “hours.”

Why D is wrong A colon would announce that the second clause explains the first. It does not; it supplies a comparison, and a semicolon is the mark for that.

stem_html:
Although the alloy was patented in 1932 and used in aircraft within the decade ______ mechanism of its resistance to fatigue was not explained until the 1970s.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", the"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ": the", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two dates and two verbs make the opening feel independent.
  • The first word decides the sentence.
  • Contrast invites a strong mark that the grammar forbids.

Why A is right “Although” makes everything before the blank a subordinate clause, and an introductory subordinate clause is followed by a comma.

Why B is wrong A semicolon needs an independent clause on its left, and this one begins with a subordinator.

Why C is wrong The introductory clause is long, and Standard English separates it from the main clause with a comma.

Why D is wrong A colon has the same requirement as the semicolon, and the relationship here is concessive rather than explanatory.

stem_html:
The oldest surviving copy of the treaty, a vellum sheet held in Seville ______ the signatures of only four of the eleven parties named in the text.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", carries"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "carries", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "; carries", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": " carrying", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The opening comma is already printed.
  • A place name immediately before the blank.
  • The participle reads smoothly and is a fragment.

Why A is right The appositive describing the copy opened with a comma after “treaty,” so it must be closed with one before the verb resumes.

Why B is wrong With the appositive left open, “Seville” appears to be what carries the signatures.

Why C is wrong A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb and leave the second part without a subject.

Why D is wrong A participle leaves the sentence with no finite verb, so it becomes a fragment.

stem_html:
The census asked one question the parish registers never had ______ where each household's members had been born.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ": where"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; where", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": ", where", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "where", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “One question” is a promise the colon keeps.
  • “Where” can open an adverbial or a noun clause, and the punctuation decides which.
  • The material after the break is not a sentence.

Why A is right The first clause is complete and names a question without stating it; a colon after an independent clause introduces the specification.

Why B is wrong A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and what follows is a noun clause rather than a sentence.

Why C is wrong A comma would attach the clause to “had” as an adverbial of place, which produces a different and false reading.

Why D is wrong With no punctuation the reader takes “where” as modifying “never had” and the sentence has to be reparsed.

stem_html:
Not one of the fourteen letters that survive from the poet's final decade ______ the illness that her biographers treat as the central fact of those years.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "mentions"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "mention", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have mentioned", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "were mentioning", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Not one” is singular however many things it is drawn from.
  • A number word and a relative clause both sit between subject and verb.
  • The singular sounds odd aloud, which is why the rule has to be applied.

Why A is right The subject is “not one,” which is singular. “Of the fourteen letters” is a prepositional phrase and the relative clause modifies “letters,” not the subject.

Why B is wrong Plural agreement follows “letters,” the nearest noun and the one inside the prepositional phrase.

Why C is wrong Plural again, and the present perfect is unmotivated in a statement about what the letters contain.

Why D is wrong The past progressive describes an action in progress, which a letter's contents are not.

stem_html:
Restored from a single surviving print and shown for the first time in ninety years, ______

The gallery hung the study beside the finished canvas so that visitors could compare ______ handling of the same shoulder.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the study's and the canvas's"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "its", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "their", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "it's", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A comparison needs two named sides.
  • A plural possessive merges the two things instead of contrasting them.
  • The apostrophe that is never possessive.

Why A is right The comparison is between two works, so both possessors have to be named. A single pronoun cannot express a comparison of two things with each other.

Why B is wrong “Its” is singular and could refer to either work, which leaves the sentence with nothing to compare.

Why C is wrong “Their” treats the two works as one possessor, which again removes the comparison the sentence exists to make.

Why D is wrong “It's” means “it is” and cannot be possessive.

Bringing a drug to market is usually described as a decade-long process, and the figure is taken from the average across all approvals. ______ that average is pulled up by a small number of chronic-disease programmes; the median oncology approval in the last five years took under six years from first-in-human trial.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A statistic and its correction.
  • “For example” is the near-miss, since a specific field does follow a general claim.
  • Consequence where there is contrast.

Why A is right The second sentence corrects the impression the first leaves, and does so with a sharper figure. “In fact” introduces the correction.

Why B is wrong “Therefore” would make the median oncology figure a consequence of the ten-year average, which is backwards.

Why C is wrong “Likewise” claims the sentences agree, and the second undercuts the first.

Why D is wrong Oncology is offered not as an instance of the decade-long process but as a case where the process is much shorter.

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A further fact, not a reversal.
  • “Neither” covers both partners, so no contrast between them is being drawn.
  • Consequence against example.

Why A is right The third sentence adds a striking further fact that deepens the point about partnership. A transition of emphasis carries it.

Why B is wrong “Nevertheless” would set the third sentence against the second, but the dependence it describes follows naturally from the division of labour just described.

Why C is wrong The inability to grow alone is not an example of the division of labour; it is a further consequence of it.

Why D is wrong “By contrast” needs two things being compared, and the third sentence covers both partners at once.
